name_en: Video-call sextortion with fake police / YouTube officials
summary: A stranger befriends the victim on social media or a dating app (or simply places an unknown WhatsApp video call), appears nude or plays an adult clip, and screen-records the victim, sometimes morphing the footage. The victim is then threatened that the video will be sent to family/contacts or uploaded, and follow-up callers pose as police officers (e.g. a 'cyber crime inspector' or 'SP' claiming the woman attempted suicide) or as YouTube staff who will 'delete the video' for a fee, extracting repeated payments.
victim_profile: Sources describe mostly men contacted through social media, dating apps or unknown WhatsApp video calls; police note both men and women can be targeted.
indicators: unknown or new contact initiates a WhatsApp video call that turns sexual
threat to send a recorded or morphed video to family or contacts
a 'police officer' or 'YouTube official' calls about the same video demanding money
repeated escalating demands after a first small payment
payment framed as settling a case or deleting a video
typical_claims: your video is recorded and will go viral if you do not pay
I am an inspector from the cyber crime cell; a case will be filed against you
the woman in the video attempted suicide and her family has evidence
I am from YouTube; pay and we will delete the uploaded video
you will lose your job if this comes out
coaching_phrases: pay a fee so the video is deleted from YouTube
pay to have the police case settled or closed
keep paying in instalments to stop the video being released
red_flag_questions: Is this payment connected to a video call or a threat to share a video of you?
Has anyone claiming to be police or YouTube asked you to pay to close a case or delete content?
Did you meet the person receiving this money online recently?
Have you already paid this person or account before, and are they asking for more?
cues_hi: आपका वीडियो रिकॉर्ड हो गया है

trend.note: Bhopal Cyber Crime police described a rapid rise in sextortion cases in Nov 2025; no national figure verified.

official_truth: I4C's advice for sextortion is do not pay, because paying only leads to further demands; report it at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930, and remember real police never settle cases for money over the phone.
advice: Do not pay; payment only brings more demands
Save chats, numbers and the video link as evidence
Report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in and to local cyber police
Do not answer video calls from unknown numbers
applicability_note: Victim personally pushes repeated UPI/bank transfers under shame and fear; a held payment plus a calm call can break the cycle.

name_en: Fake 'your child is arrested / in an accident' emergency call
summary: A caller posing as police, CBI or a hospital/legal official tells a parent that their son or daughter (often studying or working away, sometimes abroad) has been arrested in a rape or drugs case, kidnapped, or has caused a serious accident. A crying voice or a voice resembling the child is played, the parent is told not to hang up, not to contact the child and not to tell anyone, and is pushed to transfer money immediately to 'settle' the case or secure release.
victim_profile: Parents and elderly relatives of students or of children living in other cities or abroad (e.g. Canada, US), per police and news reports.
indicators: call from an unknown, foreign or WhatsApp number claiming the child is in custody or in an accident
crying or distressed voice played as proof
instruction not to disconnect and not to contact the child or anyone else
demand to pay to settle a case with police or the victim's family
claim the child's phone has been taken by police
multiple payment numbers or accounts given
typical_claims: your son has been arrested in a rape case
your daughter is in police custody with drugs
your son in Canada has caused an accident and someone is in a coma
pay now and we will settle the matter with senior officers
your son's phone is with the police, you cannot talk to him
coaching_phrases: do not hang up the call
do not contact your son; his phone is with the police
do not tell anyone or report it, just pay to settle the matter
red_flag_questions: Is this payment because someone called saying a family member is arrested, kidnapped or in an accident?
Have you been able to speak to your child directly on their own number since the call?
Were you told not to hang up or not to tell anyone in your family?
Is the money meant to settle a police case or pay someone's family?
cues_en: they said my son was arrested
cues_hinglish: aapka beta arrest ho gaya hai
rape case mein naam aaya hai
cues_hi: आपका बेटा गिरफ्तार हो गया है
रेप केस में नाम आया है

trend.note: Repeated police advisories and cases reported 2024-2025 across Goa, Chandigarh, Punjab and Andaman; no national figure verified.

official_truth: Police do not take money over the phone to drop a case or release anyone; hang up and call your child directly on their own number.
advice: Hang up and call the child or family directly on a number you already have
Do not send money to settle any 'case' over the phone
Report the number on 1930, cybercrime.gov.in or Sanchar Saathi
applicability_note: Parent personally sends UPI/bank transfers under panic; a hold that lets them reach the child usually collapses the story.

name_en: AI-cloned voice of a relative asking for urgent money
summary: Scammers collect a short voice sample of a person from social media videos or a 'wrong number' call, clone it with AI, and then call that person's parents, relatives or friends sounding distressed (sobbing, under threat, in hospital) to ask for immediate money. Urgency and emotion are used to stop the victim from checking with the real person, and payment is usually requested via UPI to an unfamiliar account.
victim_profile: Parents, elderly relatives and acquaintances of people whose voice is available online; reported cases include a Noida mother and a 67-year-old Kolkata man.
indicators: voice of a known person calling from an unknown number
sobbing or panicked tone and claim of threat, hospital or arrest
request for immediate UPI payment to an account not in the relative's name
caller resists verification or call-back
odd word choices or form of address unlike the real person
typical_claims: Mummy, I am in trouble, send money right now
I have been caught, please transfer quickly
a relative is admitted in hospital and needs money urgently
my phone is not working, this is a friend's number
coaching_phrases: pay immediately by UPI without taking time to verify
do not call back on the old number, use this new number
red_flag_questions: Did this request come from a phone call where a family member's voice asked for money?
Have you called that person back on the number you have always used for them?
Is the money going to an account in that family member's own name?
Was the call from a new or unknown number?
cues_hi: दोस्त के फोन से कॉल कर रहा हूँ

trend.note: Police advisories from 2024 and cases into 2026; the Pioneer (Sep 2026) notes no separate national figure exists for AI voice-clone fraud.

official_truth: I4C warns that a caller can sound exactly like your child using AI-cloned voice, so never act on an emergency money request without confirming through another channel or a family code word.
advice: Hang up and call the person back on their known number
Ask a question only the real person would know or use a family code word
Never pay to a new account just because the voice sounds familiar
Report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
applicability_note: Victim initiates a UPI transfer within minutes; a short hold and call-back prompt is exactly the verification police recommend.

name_en: Matrimonial-site fraud (fake NRI / doctor / army groom or bride)
summary: Fraudsters create attractive fake profiles on matrimonial sites and apps, posing as NRIs, doctors, engineers, army officers or rich businesspeople, and quickly build an emotional bond and talk of marriage. Once trusted they ask for money on pretexts such as customs duty on a gift or on currency they were 'caught' with at the airport (often voiced by a fake airport/customs official), travel or visa costs, medical emergencies, or 'investment', and keep inventing new fees until the victim stops.
victim_profile: Prospective brides and grooms on matrimonial platforms; I4C notes fraudsters screen targets by age, income and profession. Reported cases involve women professionals.
indicators: match claims to live abroad or be a doctor/army officer and avoids video calls or meeting
marriage proposed very quickly
money requested for customs, gift clearance, visa, ticket or emergency
a third party 'airport/customs official' calls asking for fees
payment to a personal account unrelated to customs
typical_claims: I have sent you expensive gifts and cash, just pay the customs charges
I am detained at Mumbai airport with foreign currency, pay the clearance fee
I need money for my visa and ticket to come to India
if you love me, please help me now
I trust only you
invest with me on this crypto platform for our future
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for someone you met on a matrimonial site or app?
Have you met this person face to face or on a live video call?
Is the money for customs duty, a gift parcel, a visa or an airport clearance?
Is the account in the name of a government department or of an individual?
cues_hinglish: pyaar karti ho toh madad karo

trend.note: I4C's threat analytics unit reported a rise in misuse of matrimonial platforms (advisory TAU/ADV/006, 31 Oct 2025, based on NCRP complaint analysis) and I4C re-issued a public warning in July 2026; no case counts given.

official_truth: I4C advises never transferring money to someone met only through a matrimonial site or app, whatever the reason given, before meeting and verifying them in person.
advice: Do not send money before meeting in person and verifying identity
Reverse-image-search profile photos and verify job claims
Treat any customs or gift fee request as a scam
Report the profile to the platform and to 1930
applicability_note: Victim makes repeated voluntary transfers to new payees for fees; a hold with the 'met in person?' question fits well.

name_en: Romance / friendship scam via dating apps and social media
summary: Fraudsters use fake or stolen-photo profiles on dating apps (Tinder, Bumble), Instagram and Facebook, posing as doctors, businesspeople, NRIs or defence personnel, and spend weeks or months building an emotional relationship. They then ask for money for sudden medical emergencies, business losses or family problems, or steer the victim into a fake 'investment'; a related in-person variant lures dating-app matches to a cafe or pub where the victim is coerced into paying a hugely inflated bill.
victim_profile: Users of dating apps, Instagram and matrimonial sites; I4C notes targets are filtered by age and income. Reported cases include women targeted by a serial conman and men lured by female profiles.
indicators: online-only partner never met in person asks for money
sudden emergency (hospital, business loss, family crisis) right after trust is built
refuses live video call or keeps changing identity
pushes a crypto or trading 'investment' together
first date at a venue chosen by the match followed by an enormous bill
asks to move the chat off the dating app to WhatsApp or phone quickly
avoids in-person meetings or video verification
typical_claims: my mother is in hospital, I need money urgently
my business account is frozen, I will return it next week
I love you and trust only you
let us invest together for our future
it is my birthday, meet me at this cafe
send me some private photos, I trust you
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for someone you know only online, through an app or social media?
Have you met this person face to face or verified them on a live video call?
Have they asked for money before for an emergency or an investment?
Did the request come soon after they told you about a crisis?

trend.note: I4C's threat analytics unit flagged dating/matrimonial-profile fraud as a latest trend in Nov 2025; large 2026 police cases reported in Delhi and Andhra Pradesh.

official_truth: I4C advises never sending money or financial details to anyone you have not met in person, and verifying their identity (for example by reverse image search) first.
advice: Do not send money to anyone known only online
Reverse-image-search the profile photos
Meet first dates in places you choose and check menu prices
Report to 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in; stigma should not stop reporting
applicability_note: Victim sends repeated voluntary transfers to the online partner; the cafe-bill variant is coerced at the venue and only partially holdable.

name_en: Gift from foreign friend stuck at customs
summary: A new Facebook/Instagram friend or online partner claiming to live in the UK or another foreign country promises to send expensive gifts, jewellery or foreign currency. A caller posing as a customs officer (or 'diplomatic agent') at Mumbai or Delhi airport then says the parcel is held and demands customs duty, clearance or penalty fees into a bank or UPI account, escalating with new charges and threats of legal action until the victim stops paying.
victim_profile: Sources describe mainly women (often homemakers) befriended on Facebook, and people on matrimonial sites; men befriended by 'foreign women' have also been targeted.
indicators: foreign online friend promises costly gifts or cash
call from a 'customs officer' at an airport about a parcel
duty or clearance fee to be paid into a personal bank account or UPI ID
fees keep rising (currency found, penalty, anti-money laundering)
threat of arrest or legal action if fees not paid
photos/videos of the gift sent on WhatsApp
fake customs receipts, courier tracking pages or photos of the gift
typical_claims: I have sent you a gift with jewellery, a phone and pounds
this is Mumbai airport customs, your parcel is held, pay the duty
the parcel contains foreign currency, you must pay a penalty
pay the clearance fee or you will face legal action
the gift is worth lakhs, the fee is small
coaching_phrases: pay the customs charges and GST now or the parcel will be confiscated
red_flag_questions: Is this payment to release a parcel or gift from abroad?
Did someone you met online promise to send you this gift?
Is the duty being paid into a personal account rather than an official customs portal?
Has the amount asked increased since your first payment?

trend.note: CBIC launched a national awareness campaign in June 2024 against frauds in the name of Customs; cases continue to be reported; no national count verified.

official_truth: Indian Customs never calls, texts or emails asking for duty to be paid into a personal bank account, and genuine customs communications carry a DIN you can verify on the CBIC website.
advice: Never pay 'customs duty' to a personal account or UPI ID
Verify any customs notice by its DIN on the CBIC website
Do not accept gifts or money offers from online friends you have not met
Report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
applicability_note: Victim pays duty/fees herself by UPI or transfer to personal accounts, repeatedly; a hold can state the CBIC fact.

name_en: Fake army / CISF buyer or seller on OLX and Facebook Marketplace
summary: Fraudsters pose as Army, CISF or paramilitary personnel on classifieds such as OLX, Quikr and social-media marketplaces. As 'buyers' they agree to the seller's price, claim a remote posting so they can only pay online, send a fake payment screenshot and then QR codes or links that, when the seller enters the UPI PIN, debit the seller repeatedly; as 'sellers' they list cheap vehicles or goods because of a transfer, send fake service ID cards and collect advances and add-on charges without delivering.
victim_profile: People selling or buying used goods, vehicles and furniture on online classifieds; sources note even service personnel have been debited.
indicators: buyer or seller says they are in the army/CISF and recently transferred
refuses in-person inspection or meeting, citing camp rules
sends an army ID card or Aadhaar as proof
seller is asked to scan a QR code or enter UPI PIN to 'receive' money
fake payment screenshot followed by 'technical issue'
advance or extra charges demanded before delivery
typical_claims: I am in the army, I am posted far away so I will pay online
I have paid, see the screenshot; there is a technical issue
scan this QR code to receive your money
outsiders are not allowed in the camp, pay the advance and we will deliver
it was a mistake, scan this one to get the refund
coaching_phrases: scan the QR code and enter your UPI PIN to receive the payment
send a small amount first to verify the account
pay the advance now because you cannot visit the camp
red_flag_questions: Are you selling or buying something online right now, and is this payment part of that deal?
Did the other person say they are in the army or a security force?
Are you being asked to scan a QR code or enter your PIN in order to receive money?
Have you seen the item or met the person in person?

trend.note: Widely reported 2019-2020 (Tamil Nadu cyber cell: about 100 complaints Jan-Sep 2020); Delhi Police still lists it; no recent national figure verified.

official_truth: You never need to scan a QR code or enter your UPI PIN to receive money; entering the PIN only ever sends money out of your account.
advice: Never scan a QR code or enter a PIN to receive a payment
Inspect the item and meet the person before paying any advance
Ignore army or government ID cards sent on WhatsApp as proof
Report to 1930 and the platform
applicability_note: Seller unknowingly authorises outgoing UPI collect/QR payments and buyers pay advances; both are victim-initiated and holdable.

name_en: Rental fraud by fake army / NSG tenant (send money to receive the rent advance)
summary: After an owner lists a flat on a real-estate portal or social media, a caller posing as an Army, NSG or CRPF officer 'being transferred' agrees to rent it without visiting and sends a uniformed photo and forged ID. A 'senior officer' or 'Army accountant' then says defence payment rules require a 'reversal mode' or a payment to 'raise a demand', gets the owner to send a small test amount (sometimes returned to build trust), then the advance and ever larger sums, or to click payment links, promising everything will be refunded with the rent. Police also report fake rental listings that take advances from would-be tenants, but the documented army-officer cases mostly target owners.
victim_profile: Property owners advertising flats for rent on housing portals and social media, per Hyderabad and Andaman & Nicobar police.
indicators: prospective tenant claims to be army/NSG/CRPF and recently transferred
agrees to rent without seeing the property
a 'senior officer' or 'army accountant' handles the payment
owner asked to pay first, send a test amount, or type the advance amount into a link
'system failure' leads to repeated transfers with promised refunds
uniformed DP, patriotic slogans, forged service ID
a UPI request-money / collect notification arrives that you are told to approve to receive the deposit
typical_claims: I am an army officer transferred here, I will take the flat without visiting
our accountant will pay the advance through army reversal mode
send Rs 5 first to test, it will come back
due to defence security protocol you must pay to raise the demand
the system failed, send again and everything will be refunded
coaching_phrases: send a small test amount first; it will be credited back
pay the amount to 'raise a demand' so the army system releases the advance
keep transferring until the system acknowledges and refunds everything
enter the advance amount yourself in the payment link
the deposit can only come from the Army bank, so add our UPI ID and approve the request
red_flag_questions: Is this payment connected to renting out or renting a property?
Has the person paying or receiving rent said they are from the army or a security force?
Are you being asked to send money so that you can receive an advance or refund?
Has the tenant or landlord seen the property or met you in person?
cues_hinglish: army officer flat lena chahta hai
advance ke liye pehle paise bhejo
cues_hi: एडवांस के लिए पहले पैसे भेजो

trend.note: Police advisories in 2024 (Andaman & Nicobar) and repeated Hyderabad cases in 2025; no national figure verified.

official_truth: I4C states that entering a UPI PIN or OTP is needed only to send money, never to receive it, so no genuine tenant needs you to pay or approve a request to get a rent advance.
advice: Never send money to receive an advance or refund
Insist on a physical visit and verify the tenant independently
Ignore uniform photos and service IDs shared on WhatsApp
Report to 1930 immediately
applicability_note: Owner makes repeated outbound IMPS/UPI transfers believing they enable a credit; a hold that asks 'are you paying to receive?' maps directly.

name_en: KBC lottery / lucky draw / brand anniversary prize
summary: A WhatsApp message, audio, call or poster (often from +92 or other foreign numbers, using KBC, Jio, celebrity or brand logos) says the recipient has won a lottery such as Rs 25 lakh, or a brand 'anniversary gift'/lucky draw. To claim it the victim must contact a 'lottery manager' and pay processing charges, GST, income tax or transfer fees into various bank accounts; the prize is 'increased' to keep them paying for weeks. Brand-gift links instead lead to fake look-alike portals that harvest money and personal data.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (cases include homemakers and young adults).
indicators: you 'won' a lottery or draw you never entered
message from a foreign (+92) number using KBC, Jio or celebrity images
fee, GST or tax must be paid before the prize is released
payments to several different personal bank accounts
prize amount keeps increasing with new charges
told to talk only on WhatsApp and keep it secret
typical_claims: congratulations, your number has won Rs 25 lakh in the KBC Jio lottery
call our lottery manager on WhatsApp to claim
pay the refundable processing fee and GST first
your prize has increased to Rs 45 lakh, pay the extra tax
brand anniversary offer: you are the lucky winner, click to claim your gift
coaching_phrases: contact the manager only on WhatsApp
keep the prize secret until it is credited
pay the processing fee and GST first; it is refundable
red_flag_questions: Is this payment to claim a prize, lottery or gift?
Did you enter this lottery or draw yourself?
Are you being asked to pay tax or fees before receiving winnings?
Have you discussed this with your family?
cues_en: they said i won a lottery
cues_hinglish: tax bharne ke baad paisa milega
cues_hi: आपकी 25 लाख की लॉटरी लगी है
टैक्स भरने के बाद पैसा मिलेगा

trend.note: Long-running; Delhi Police maintains a dedicated KBC page and Kerala Police warned of brand 'anniversary gift' links in June 2026; no national figure verified.

official_truth: Genuine lotteries deduct any tax from the prize itself and never ask winners to pay fees or GST in advance; KBC does not run WhatsApp lotteries.
advice: Never pay any fee or tax to receive a prize
Ignore prize messages from unknown or foreign numbers
Check offers only on the brand's official website
Report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
applicability_note: Victim makes repeated voluntary fee transfers; brand-gift phishing links are only partially holdable.

name_en: Fake donation drive (temple, disaster relief, needy person)
summary: During disasters (floods, landslides), major religious events (e.g. the Ayodhya Ram temple consecration) or via hijacked friends' social-media accounts, fraudsters circulate appeals with QR codes, UPI IDs or bank accounts that imitate official relief funds or temple trusts, or ask for help for a 'needy person'. Look-alike UPI IDs that differ by one letter from an official fund, and QR codes sent privately on WhatsApp, route the donation to the fraudster.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (devotees and well-wishers responding to disasters or religious events).
indicators: donation QR code or UPI ID received on WhatsApp or social media rather than an official portal
UPI ID or payee name slightly different from the official relief fund or trust
caller or page asks for your WhatsApp number to send a QR code
appeal timed to a disaster or big religious event
request for money for a 'needy person' from a friend's account
typical_claims: donate for the Ram temple construction, scan this QR code
contribute to flood relief through this UPI ID
give your WhatsApp number and I will send the donation QR
help this needy family urgently
the trust is collecting donations through this account
red_flag_questions: Is this payment a donation to a temple, relief fund or charity?
Where did you get this QR code or UPI ID: an official website, or a WhatsApp/social media message?
Does the payee name exactly match the official fund or trust?
Did someone call or message you asking you to donate?

trend.note: Spikes around disasters and major religious events (e.g. Dec 2023-Jan 2024 Ram temple warnings); no figures verified.

official_truth: Police advise donating only through the official website or verified account of the relief fund or trust, since fraudsters circulate look-alike QR codes and UPI IDs.
advice: Donate only via the official portal or verified account
Check the UPI ID and payee name letter by letter
Ignore donation QR codes sent on WhatsApp or by unknown callers
Report fake appeals on 1930
applicability_note: Donor initiates the UPI payment; a check of the payee name against the official fund is a natural hold question, though amounts are often small.

name_en: Fake shopping / sale website or social-media shop
summary: Fraudsters build look-alike websites of known brands, restaurants or new 'stores' and promote them through social-media and search ads with very deep discounts on phones, electronics, shoes or food. The buyer pays online (UPI, card or transfer) but nothing is delivered, a used or different item arrives, or card details are harvested; some sites promise a free gift and then a fake customer-service caller demands refundable handling or GST fees. Sites change their URLs when reported.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (online shoppers attracted by deep discounts).
indicators: price far below the market for a high-value item
site reached through a social-media or search ad, recently created domain or misspelled brand name
only prepaid payment, no cash on delivery, or payment to a personal UPI ID
no reviews or many non-delivery complaints
'customer care' calls asking for extra handling, GST or gift-release fees
typical_claims: mega sale: iPhone at 80% off, today only
limited stock, pay now to confirm the order
free gift with your order, pay the refundable handling charge
cash on delivery not available for this offer
your order is on hold until you pay GST
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for an online purchase? Which website or app?
How did you find the site: an ad on social media or a message?
Is the price much lower than on well-known sites?
Is the payment going to a company account or to an individual's UPI ID?

trend.note: MHA told Parliament (Jul 2024) that fake-website fraud is not recorded separately by NCRB; I4C had disabled 91 phishing/fake websites and NIXI 310 malicious .in domains by then.

official_truth: You can check whether a website has been reported as suspect on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) before paying, and police advise that offers that look too good to be true usually are.
advice: Buy only from known sites or the brand's official app
Prefer cash on delivery on new or unknown sites
Check the URL spelling and reviews, and check the site on cybercrime.gov.in
Report the site via 'Report Suspect' on cybercrime.gov.in or 1930
applicability_note: UPI/transfer to a personal payee is holdable; card payments through a gateway on a fake site may not route through Ruko.

summary: Fraudsters set up websites or social-media pages that copy a well-known brand (for example a dairy cooperative, fuel company or consumer brand) or a government-style portal and invite people to apply for a franchise, dealership or distributorship. Applicants are then asked to pay registration, application, security deposit, documentation or 'tax' fees in stages into bank accounts, after which the fraudsters vanish. A related I4C-documented variant is a 'foreign investor' offering a business partnership who first needs deposits for documentation and customs.
victim_profile: general public; no specific profile documented (aspiring business owners responding to online ads).
indicators: franchise or dealership offer found via an ad, social media or a look-alike website rather than the brand's official site
registration, approval or security-deposit fee demanded upfront to a bank account or UPI ID
pressure to pay quickly to 'reserve' a location
use of brand logos or government emblems as proof
payee name is an individual or unrelated company
typical_claims: your application for the dealership is approved, pay the registration fee
pay the security deposit to confirm your location
limited franchises available in your district
pay documentation and tax charges before the agreement is issued
I am an investor abroad looking for a trusted business partner in India
red_flag_questions: Is this payment a fee for a franchise, dealership or distributorship?
Where did you apply: on the company's official website, or through a link, ad or call?
Have you verified the offer by calling the company on a number from its official website?
Is the payee the company itself or an individual account?

trend.note: No fetched source gives figures; brand and police warnings exist but are undated.

official_truth: Brands warn that fraudsters copy their names and logos on fake websites, so never pay any franchise or registration fee unless you have verified the offer directly with the company through its official website.
advice: Apply only through the company's official website and verify by phone
Never pay registration or deposit fees to personal accounts
Check suspicious portals with PIB Fact Check or on cybercrime.gov.in
Report to 1930
applicability_note: Applicant voluntarily sends staged fees by transfer; a hold asking how the offer was verified fits. Note: no fetched source specifically documents petrol-pump/LPG dealership cases.

name_en: Fake pilgrimage / travel booking (Kedarnath helicopter, Char Dham, hotels, cabs)
summary: Fraudsters run fake websites, social-media pages, WhatsApp accounts and even paid Google/Facebook ads offering Kedarnath helicopter tickets, Char Dham yatra packages, guest-house and hotel rooms, cabs and religious tour packages, often misusing names of real booking platforms. Pilgrims and tourists pay by UPI or transfer to confirm, receive fake tickets or nothing, and the contact goes silent.
victim_profile: Religious pilgrims and tourists, per the I4C alert.
indicators: helicopter or darshan booking offered outside the official IRCTC/state portal
booking found via a sponsored search ad or social-media page
payment requested to a personal UPI ID or individual's account
very cheap or 'guaranteed' tickets during peak season
agent communicates only on WhatsApp and sends a ticket image
typical_claims: Kedarnath helicopter tickets available, confirm now with advance
guaranteed Char Dham package, limited seats
pay the full amount by UPI and we will send the ticket on WhatsApp
hotel near the temple, pay 50% advance to block the room
official booking agent, IRCTC quota
red_flag_questions: Is this payment for a pilgrimage, helicopter, hotel or tour booking?
Did you find the booking through a search ad, social media or WhatsApp rather than the official portal?
Is the payment going to an individual's UPI ID or account?
Have you checked the booking on the official IRCTC or state portal?

trend.note: I4C issued a nationwide alert on online booking frauds targeting pilgrims and tourists (summarised in a 2025 CRPF newsletter); no figures verified.

official_truth: Kedarnath Dham helicopter services can be booked only through the official IRCTC website, and I4C has warned that fake sites, pages and sponsored ads target pilgrims.
advice: Book helicopter and darshan services only on official portals
Do not trust sponsored ads or WhatsApp agents for pilgrimage bookings
Check the URL spelling and never pay a personal UPI ID
Report fake sites on cybercrime.gov.in or 1930
applicability_note: Pilgrim pays an advance by UPI/transfer to an individual; a hold that asks whether it was booked on the official portal fits.

name_en: Hacked or cloned friend's account asking for urgent money
summary: Fraudsters take over a person's WhatsApp account (by tricking them into sharing the activation OTP or merging a verification call) or hijack/clone their Facebook or Instagram profile, sometimes using a senior officer's photo as display picture. They then message the victim's contacts and groups saying they are in hospital, stuck in an emergency or need urgent payment, promising to repay in a day or two, and ask for money to a UPI ID or bank account that is not the friend's.
victim_profile: Friends, relatives and colleagues of the person whose account was hijacked or cloned; general public.
indicators: money request by chat from a known contact with no call
new number or duplicate profile of an existing friend
claims to be unable to talk (in a meeting, phone problem, hospital)
asks to pay a third party's UPI ID or account
promise to repay within a day or two
message tone, spelling or language unlike the real person
typical_claims: I am hospitalised, please transfer money urgently
I am in a meeting, can't talk, please send to this account
my old number has a problem, this is my new number
I will return it tomorrow
send to my friend's UPI, my GPay is not working
coaching_phrases: don't call me, I am in a meeting; just send to this account
send it to this other person's UPI ID, mine is not working
I will repay you in a day or two
I sent you an OTP by mistake, please forward it to me
red_flag_questions: Did this request come by chat or social media from a friend or colleague?
Have you spoken to that person on a voice call on their usual number?
Is the money going to an account in their own name?
Did they say they cannot talk right now?
cues_hinglish: dost ke UPI pe bhej do
cues_hi: गलती से ओटीपी आया है बता दो

trend.note: I4C advisory (2022) and BPRD advisory (Jan 2024) both describe it; no figures verified.

official_truth: I4C and Delhi Police advise treating any money request over chat as suspect and calling the person directly on their known number before paying, because hijacked accounts are used to message all contacts.
advice: Call the friend on their known number before sending anything
Never share a WhatsApp code or OTP with anyone
Turn on WhatsApp two-step verification
Report the account to the platform and to 1930
applicability_note: Contact pushes a UPI/transfer to a third-party account; a hold with 'have you spoken to them by voice?' is decisive.

name_en: Boss / CEO / senior officer impersonation on WhatsApp
summary: Fraudsters message employees or subordinates from a new number using the boss's photo as display picture, or from the boss's genuine WhatsApp account after hijacking it (I4C's 2026 'Boss Scam': malicious 'Statement of Account'/RBI/MCA zip files take over WhatsApp Web), or save their own number under 'CEO' on a compromised phone. Claiming to be busy, travelling or in a meeting, they instruct urgent fund transfers to mule accounts or the purchase of gift cards (e.g. Amazon) whose codes must be sent back, citing client gifts, staff incentives or confidential deals.
victim_profile: Finance and accounts staff, CFOs, Chartered Accountants and company directors (per I4C), and subordinates of senior officers or executives.
indicators: urgent payment or gift-card request from the 'boss' over WhatsApp or email only
new number with the boss's photo, or 'CEO' contact that changed recently
sender says they are in a meeting or travelling and cannot take calls
payee is a new beneficiary or individual account
request to send gift card codes as photos
request arrives right after a zip file was opened on a work computer
typical_claims: I am in a meeting, process this payment immediately
buy Amazon gift cards for clients and send me the codes
I am travelling and unreachable, handle this urgently
use this new account for the vendor
forward this statement file to the finance manager for verification
coaching_phrases: I am busy in a meeting, do not call, just process it
I am travelling and unreachable, handle it urgently
send the gift card codes back to me on chat
red_flag_questions: Is this payment on instructions received from a senior person over WhatsApp or email?
Have you confirmed it with them by a direct voice call or in person?
Is the beneficiary new or different from the usual account?
Are you being asked to buy gift cards or vouchers?
cues_hinglish: gift card kharid ke code bhejo
cues_hi: बॉस ने ट्रांसफर करने को कहा

trend.note: PIB/I4C (7 Aug 2026) reported a sharp rise in NCRP complaints from several States and said it alerted over 58,000 potential victims in 30 days.

official_truth: I4C advises that any urgent fund-transfer or account-change instruction received over WhatsApp or email must be independently verified by a direct voice call or in person before acting on it.
advice: Call the senior person on their known number before paying
Never buy gift cards on a chat instruction
Follow normal approval steps for new beneficiaries
Do not open zip/exe files claiming to be statements or RBI notices; report to 1930
applicability_note: Bank transfers to mule accounts are holdable; gift-card purchases by card may not pass through Ruko.

name_en: Fake recovery agent / 'cyber cell' / lawyer promising to recover lost money
summary: After someone has lost money to a scam, they are contacted (or find online) people posing as a government agency, cyber cell, law firm or consumer body, or even the original company, who claim they can recover or are holding the lost money. The victim is asked to pay an upfront retainer, processing fee, tax or 'release' charge, or to share bank details, and loses more money. Documented in this run by the US FTC; the Indian 'fake cyber cell / lawyer' variant could not be verified from a fetched Indian source.
victim_profile: People who have already lost money to a scam, per the FTC (scammers buy lists of prior victims).
indicators: unsolicited contact referring to your earlier fraud loss
caller claims to be cyber cell, police, government, lawyer or recovery agency
upfront fee, tax or 'release charge' required before the refund
guarantee that the money will be recovered
payment asked by UPI/transfer to an individual, gift card or crypto
typical_claims: we have traced and frozen your lost money
pay the processing fee and the amount will be released
we are from the cyber cell, the refund is approved
our lawyers guarantee full recovery
pay the tax first to receive your refund
red_flag_questions: Have you recently lost money to a fraud, and is this payment meant to get it back?
Who contacted you about recovering it, and did they contact you first?
Are you being asked to pay a fee, tax or charge before the money is returned?
Have you checked the status through your 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in complaint or your bank instead?

trend.note: No Indian trend data verified in this run.

official_truth: In India, money frozen after a 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in complaint is returned through banks and police under the MHA's restoration procedure, and consumer authorities warn that anyone demanding an upfront fee to recover lost money is a scammer.
advice: Never pay an upfront fee to recover lost money
Track recovery only through your 1930 complaint, the police station or your bank
Do not share bank details with recovery callers
Report the recovery caller to 1930
applicability_note: Prior victim voluntarily pays a fee; a hold can redirect them to their official 1930 complaint. Indian variant (fake cyber cell/lawyers) not verified by an Indian source in this run because the web-search budget ran out.
